title: The craftsmanship shutdown
body:
A fire shuts down your only production atelier, delaying 35% of your upcoming luxury collection. Your VIP customers have already placed pre-orders.

The twist: A mass-production manufacturer offers to fulfil the orders in half the time, but using it could compromise your craftsmanship and exclusivity.

Your plan must decide: Outsource the production, delay the collection, or compensate your customers, and what you tell your VIP clients.

title: The next-generation exodus
body:
Younger affluent consumers are abandoning traditional luxury brands for independent designers and niche labels. Your sales to customers under 35 fall 25%.

The twist: A popular independent designer offers a collaboration, but demands complete creative freedom and equal brand recognition.

Your plan must decide: Collaborate on those terms, acquire the label, or reinvent your own brand for the new generation, and how you keep your existing clients.

title: The Ambassador Scandal
body:
Your luxury fashion house has signed a five-year, ₹100 crore endorsement deal with one of the world's biggest celebrities, who represents the brand globally and features in every major campaign. An investigative report then exposes the celebrity's involvement in a major public controversy. Within 48 hours: social-media sentiment about your brand drops 30%, three major retail partners demand an explanation, pre-orders for your latest collection fall 20%, and customers start linking your brand with the controversy.

The twist: The celebrity owns 15% of your company through an earlier strategic partnership. Ending the endorsement could trigger a contractual dispute and force you to buy back their shares at a substantial premium.

Your plan must decide: Terminate the partnership immediately and accept the financial consequences; retain the celebrity and defend the partnership; or suspend the campaign while an independent investigation takes place.

title: The luxury market crash
body:
A sudden downturn cuts discretionary spending: luxury retail falls 18%, high-end hospitality bookings 25% and luxury real estate deals 30%. Your next funding round is postponed.

The twist: Your largest investor asks you to cut prices 20% to keep sales up. Your brand team says that would end the brand.

Your plan must decide: Discount, hold prices and cut costs, or launch something cheaper under another name. Show the runway.

title: The product nobody wants to sell
body:
Your affordable personal-care product is an unexpected hit: its low price attracts millions of buyers and demand grows fast across the country. But the big retail chains find that it earns them far less per metre of shelf than rival brands, and they start replacing it with more profitable products. Your research shows consumers actively prefer your product; retailers are simply unwilling to stock it.

The twist: Your biggest competitor offers retailers large incentives to remove your product entirely. At the same time, a major quick-commerce platform offers to sell it exclusively in its app, with guaranteed nationwide visibility.

Your plan must decide: Fight for traditional retail (better margins and promotions for retailers, at the cost of your profitability); go direct to consumers (build your own distribution and online sales, giving up reach now and investing heavily); or accept the platform's exclusivity (guaranteed visibility, but the platform controls customer access, pricing and distribution).

title: The secret ingredient
body:
Your flagship beverage is one of India's most successful products because of its distinctive flavour, and its formula is your biggest competitive advantage. Your chief product developer resigns and joins a competitor. Within weeks, the competitor launches a remarkably similar drink at 30% lower prices. Your sales start falling as retailers give shelf space to the cheaper drink.

The twist: The former employee had access to the complete formula. And the supplier of your drink's most distinctive ingredient has just signed an exclusive agreement with the competitor.

Your plan must decide: Fight legally (sue the competitor and the former employee, risking a long battle while market share keeps falling); reinvent the formula (a new recipe, risking rejection by consumers and the loss of the product's identity); or acquire the competitor or license from it (regain control of the formula, at a large cost and with regulatory complications).

title: Fake sustainability data
body:
A journalist shows that a key supplier faked its 'plastic-free' and 'organic' data, which you printed on your packs. #Greenwashing trends with your name in it.

The twist: You find that a second supplier may also be faking data, but checking it takes 6 weeks.

Your plan must decide: Say so now, or wait until you are sure. Who is told, and when.

title: The product that outgrew its market
body:
Your packaged snack becomes an unexpected social-media sensation and demand rises 300% in six weeks. You expand production, buy new machinery and sign distribution agreements to keep up. Then the trend fades, leaving you with ₹12 crore of unsold stock, three-year manufacturing commitments, expensive new capacity, and retailers demanding compensation for unsold stock.

The twist: A major international retailer offers to buy all the remaining stock, but only at 40% below your original wholesale price. Accepting could permanently reset what consumers expect to pay for your product.

Your plan must decide: Liquidate aggressively (accept the offer, recover cash and protect working capital, but damage your pricing power); protect the brand (refuse the discount and sell slowly through your own channels, risking expiry, waste and cash locked in stock); or reinvent the product (repackage and reposition it for a different use, investing more in a product whose popularity may be gone).

title: Grid blackout in peak summer
body:
A 9-hour blackout across 4 states. Your systems or stations go offline, 30% of customers miss service, and penalty clauses cost Rs 55 lakh.

The twist: A second blackout is likely within the week, and a minister blames 'private operators' on live TV.

Your plan must decide: Who you protect first (hospitals, paying customers, or the grid operator), and what you tell the public.

title: Cheap imports flood the market
body:
Solar panels and batteries from abroad drop 25% in price. Your hardware now costs more than rivals' and two big orders are cancelled.

The twist: An importer offers to supply you at their low price if you put your brand on their hardware.

Your plan must decide: Rebrand imports, cut your own costs, or compete on service and warranty. Show the margin of each.

title: A battery fire goes viral
body:
A video of a battery fire at a customer site gets 4 million views. The fire was not proven to be yours, but bookings fall 40% and a regulator asks for safety data.

The twist: The regulator gives you 72 hours to share your safety data, and your own data shows one near-miss you never reported.

Your plan must decide: Disclose the near-miss or not, and how you rebuild trust with customers who are scared.

title: Subsidy cut overnight
body:
The government cuts the subsidy your customers rely on from Rs 30,000 to Rs 10,000. Your payback pitch of 4 years becomes 6.5 years.

The twist: A state government offers its own subsidy, but only if you build a factory in that state within 2 years.

Your plan must decide: Take the deal, change the business model, or sell to customers who do not need the subsidy. Show the payback.

title: Grounded at Dawn
body:
An engine-inspection order grounds 22 of the 64 turboprops for 21 days. 131 of the 380 routes stop overnight. In week one, 27,000 booked passengers and 92 tonnes of booked cargo are stranded.

The twist: Operators will restore only routes that show committed demand. They want a 14-day list of confirmed bookings from partners by Friday; routes without one may be dropped for good.

Your plan must decide: What you do for your users in the first 72 hours, whether you move them to road, rail or another airline and who pays, and how you help your route prove its demand by Friday.

title: The giant comes to town
body:
The national airline with 61% market share takes 70 of the 140 best regional routes next quarter. It flies 78-seaters at a ₹1,999 launch fare and bundles its own app, cab, cargo and maintenance. Regional bookings on those routes fall 34% in a week, and 2 of the 4 operators may exit.

The twist: The giant offers every startup the same deal: a 3-year exclusive contract on its routes only. Volume triples, the unit price falls 40%, and the giant owns the customer.

Your plan must decide: Sign, refuse or negotiate; which customers you lock in before the switch; and whether you fight on the giant's routes or move to the ones it did not take.

title: Near-miss in the fog
body:
A turboprop lands in 40 m visibility at a small airport. No one is hurt, but the cockpit audio goes viral. The regulator finds 40 of the 120 airports lack working landing aids and suspends low-visibility flying there for 60 days. First-time-flyer bookings fall 30% across the network.

The twist: The regulator will name the 40 airports only in 10 days. Until then, your users and clients ask you every day: "Is my airport safe?"

Your plan must decide: What you tell users before the official list, whether you pause sales at airports you suspect, and how you win back first-time flyers once the list is out.

title: The subsidy cliff
body:
The Centre cuts route support. Subsidy on 150 of the 380 routes ends in 90 days, a year early, and operators say 90 of those routes will close unless fares rise 40%. States, now short of money, will pay all startup invoices 90 days late. Your next funding round is postponed.

The twist: One state offers to keep its 40 routes flying for 2 more years if aviation startups pay into a shared route fund: ₹25 lakh each, returned only if those routes reach 65% seat load within a year.

Your plan must decide: Pay in, stay out, or cut costs and wait. Show your cash runway under your choice.

title: The algorithm misfires
body:
A bug in your model makes 6,000 wrong trades or loan decisions in one morning. Customers lose Rs 2.1 crore before you stop it.

The twist: A customer who lost Rs 9 lakh goes on TV; your lawyers advise you to refund nobody until the cause is proven.

Your plan must decide: Refund everyone now, refund case by case, or wait. Show the cost, and what you change in the model.

title: A market crash
body:
The market falls 14% in five days. Your users' portfolios (or your borrowers' sales) drop sharply, and 25% of users stop using the app.

The twist: Influencers tell your users to 'buy the dip' with borrowed money, using your app's name.

Your plan must decide: Warn your users even if trading falls, or stay quiet. How you protect users from the worst losses.

title: A data breach
body:
Hackers leak the phone numbers and PAN details of 3 lakh users. Fraud calls start the same day and the news covers it.

The twist: The hackers claim they still have access, and your security team cannot yet prove they are wrong.

Your plan must decide: Shut the app until it is safe, or stay open with extra checks. What it costs and what users are told.

title: The regulator changes the rules
body:
The central bank tightens rules on your product: digital lending caps, new KYC checks, or limits on derivatives for small investors. Revenue from your main product falls 40%.

The twist: A rival keeps selling the old product through an offshore company and takes your users.

Your plan must decide: Follow the rules and lose users, or find a compliant product that wins them back. Show revenue for both.
